1-1

Lecture 1-1

What is a chemical process?

Where chemical engineering starts

Two types of manufacturing process

Type I — shape is changed
Raw material is re-shaped and assembled.
No change in chemical composition.
Type II — chemical structure is changed
Raw material is forced into a different chemical structure.
This is a chemical process.

Interactive — decide for each case

Type I or Type II? Judge the manufacturing route

Stamping a car door panel from a steel coil
Type I. Only the shape changes — the steel is still steel.
Steam-cracking naphtha into ethylene
Type II. C–C bonds are broken; new molecules leave the reactor.
Assembling a smartphone from modules
Type I. Each piece is assembled into the final product; composition is untouched.
Fermenting molasses into ethanol
Type II. Sugar becomes ethanol + CO₂ — a new chemical structure.
Rolling a steel slab into thin sheet
Type I. Thickness changes, chemistry does not.
Neutralising HCl with NaOH to make brine
Type II. Reactants disappear and NaCl + H₂O appear.

0 / 6 correct

What the customer buys

The product of a chemical process

The product has a different chemical structure than the raw material.
The product has a higher purity than the raw material.

Both must be true. A reactor alone changes the structure; only the separation train delivers the purity.

Distillation column
Stirred reactor

Characteristic of a chemical process

One change in structure → many process steps

Ethylbenzene / styrene flowsheet — a single chemical change spread over dozens of steps.

Multistep operation: a change in chemical structure cannot be completed in a single step — each step is a reaction, separation, mixing, heating or cooling.

Every chemical process has the same five sections

Unconverted reactant is recovered from both the phase separation and the purification section and recycled to feed preparation; what cannot be sold leaves purification for environmental control.

Section summary

Lecture 1-1 — what to carry forward

1

Type II = chemical process: the raw material is forced into a different chemical structure.

2

A saleable product needs both a new structure and a higher purity.

3

Structure change never happens in one step → the process is always multistep.

4

Process = feed prep, reactor, phase separation, purification, environmental control. Plant = process + storage + utilities + waste.

Casework 1-1 · exam-style

The licensor's flowsheet has no environmental control

A licensor offers you a process with feed preparation, reactor, phase separation, purification and recycle — and no waste treatment. The vent and the aqueous purge simply leave the battery limit.
What must your design team add, and is it part of the process or the plant?
1. Environmental control is one of the five sections inside the process boundary — vent scrubbing, purge treatment, off-gas incineration must be designed with the process, not bolted on.
2. The waste-treatment facility (bio-treatment pond, flare, WWTP) sits outside at plant level, with utilities and storage.
3. Consequence of skipping it: the overall material balance will not close on the environmental streams, and the profit margin computed in Step I is optimistic.

Redrawn from the lecture: the section the flowsheet forgot.

1-2

Lecture 1-2

What is chemical process design?

Definition

Chemical process design = six decisions

  • Select and arrange the sequence of each operation
  • Specify the operating conditions
  • Calculate the duties (energy) required to operate the process
  • Select materials of construction of all process equipment
  • Arrange the equipment so the plant functions (equipment layout)
  • Specify line sizes and principal instrumentation
Design is not one calculation. It is a sequence of decisions, each made at a level of detail the previous one has earned.

The professor's metaphor

Chemical process design vs colour painting

Start — outline only
→
Finish — full detail
A painter never starts with the darkest detail. Neither does a designer: each design step adds detail only where the previous step is already right — and the cost estimate gets sharper as the picture does.

What does each design step deliver?

 

STEP I

Input–Output Design

Deliverables:

Cost estimate:

accuracy band around the true cost  (−60% … +60% scale)

Step I · Input–Output Design (order-of-magnitude)

The process is still a single black box

  • Input / output structure
  • Overall material balance
  • Profit margin (product value − raw material cost)
If the profit margin is negative here, no amount of clever equipment design will save the project. Stop at Step I.

Step II · General Process Design (study design)

Output: the block flow diagram

1,3-propanediol production — reactors, separators, conversions and recycle now visible, but no equipment specification yet.

Step III · Conceptual Process Design (preliminary design)

Output: the process flow diagram + profit analysis

Every block has become real equipment with tags, streams and utilities — the first drawing an engineer can cost.

Step V · FEED / Definitive design (piping & instrumentation)

Now every piece of equipment is specified

Vessel sketch
Process datasheet
stream properties + dimensions
Piping & instrumentation diagram
the EPC contractor's design basis

Step VI · Detail Engineering Design (firm / contractor's estimate)

From specification to something you can build

Equipment drawing
Plant layout
3D isometric model

Plus plant arrangement and piping isometrics — the deliverables a fabricator and a construction crew work from.

Lecture 1-3

How does a real design project progress — and how good is the cost estimate at each stage?

Project phases

The design steps live inside five project phases

Plan

Identify the business opportunity · classify risks · align objectives

+50% / −30%

Select

Select the best approach · quantify economics · rank by value

+30% / −20%

Define

Finalise scope & execution plan · contracting · sanctioning

+20% / −15%

Execute

Engineering and construction management

+10% / −5%

Operate

Commissioning & operating to achieve design performance

Basic engineering covers basic design & engineering + Front-End Engineering Design (FEED) — the two are often used interchangeably in industry.

Project phases

Five estimate classes, three budget gates

Design / project stageEstimate classAccuracyBudget gate
Scope study / prelim. feasibilityOrder-of-magnitude+50% / −30%Approval 1
Conceptual process design / feasibilityStudy (factored)+30% / −20%—
Basic design & engineeringBudget authorization+20% / −15%Approval 2 (may skip)
Front-End Engineering Design (FEED)Project control (definitive)+15% / −10%Approval 3
Detailed design & engineeringDetail+10% / −5%—

Proposal + rough PFD supports the early classes; detailed sizing + P&ID is what buys the tight ones.

Casework 1-3 · exam-style

Should we skip basic design to save three months?

Your team has a study estimate of 150 M$ (+30% / −20%) from the conceptual design. Management proposes going straight to FEED, skipping basic design and engineering, to save three months.
What do they gain, what do they risk, and what would you insist on?
GainThree months of schedule, and Budget Approval 2 is explicitly a gate that may be skipped. RiskYou commit to FEED with a 120–195 M$ band still open (75 M$ wide). If the scope grows, the FEED contract itself is re-worked — the most expensive place to discover it. Insist onA frozen PFD and heat/material balance before FEED begins, plus major-equipment sizing good enough for a +20/−15% number. That is basic engineering work even if you do not call it a phase. PrincipleYou may skip the gate; you cannot skip the definition. Changes at the PFD stage are cheap — the same change during FEED is not.
1-4

Lecture 1-4

What is the important diagram in a chemical process?

Basic chemical engineering flow diagrams

Three diagrams, three levels of detail

Block Flow Diagram
(BFD)

Operations as blocks. Main flows, direction, conversions, a simplified material balance.

Answers: what happens, in what order?

Process Flow Diagram
(PFD)

Every major equipment item, tagged and named, with all process streams numbered and utilities shown.

Answers: what do we build and how much does it cost?

Piping & Instrumentation Diagram (P&ID)

Every valve, line, instrument and spare — the design basis handed to the EPC contractor.

Answers: how is it piped, controlled and made safe?

Block flow diagram

Benzene via hydrodealkylation of toluene

$\mathrm{C_7H_8 + H_2 \rightarrow C_6H_6 + CH_4}$  ·  10,000 + 820 kg/h in, 8,210 + 2,610 kg/h out — the balance closes at the block level.

Block flow diagram

Six drawing conventions

  • Operations are shown by blocks.
  • Major flow lines carry arrows giving the direction of flow.
  • Flow goes left to right wherever possible — recycles go right to left.
  • Light streams (gases) toward the top, heavy streams (liquids, solids) toward the bottom.
  • If lines cross, the horizontal line stays continuous and the vertical line is broken.
  • A simplified material balance is provided.
These conventions are not decoration — they let any engineer read your flowsheet in the direction the process actually runs.

Interactive — the same plant, three levels of detail

Zooming in: BFD → PFD → P&ID

 

Process flow diagram

Five things a PFD must show

  • All major pieces of equipment, with a description of each.
  • A unique equipment number and a descriptive name for every item.
  • All process flow streams, each identified by a number.
  • A description of the process conditions and the chemical composition of each stream.
  • All utility streams supplied to major equipment that provide a process function.
If it changes the material or energy balance, it belongs on the PFD. If it only makes the plant operable, it belongs on the P&ID.

Process flow diagram

What counts as "major equipment"?

Changes temperature

Heat exchangers, fired heaters, coolers, condensers, reboilers.

Changes pressure

Pumps, compressors, turbines, expanders, throttling for a process reason.

Changes composition

Reactors, towers, absorbers, extractors, filters, dryers.

Three questions to test any item: does it change $T$, $P$, or composition? If none of the three, it is not major — keep it off the PFD.

Process flow diagram

Identifying a process stream

  • A diamond symbol placed in the flow line.
  • A numerical identification, unique for that stream, inserted in the diamond.
  • Flow direction shown by arrows on the flow lines.
Only the diamond is required. The flag-shaped symbols are optional ways to show conditions directly on the drawing.

Process flow diagram

Stream properties: required vs optional

Required information

  • Stream number
  • Temperature (°C)
  • Pressure (bar)
  • Vapour fraction
  • Total mass flowrate (kg/h)
  • Total mole flowrate (kmol/h)
  • Individual component flowrates (kmol/h)

Optional information

  • Stream name
  • Component mole / mass fractions
  • Component flowrates (kg/h), volumetric flowrate (m³/h)
  • Physical properties: density, viscosity
  • Thermodynamic data: heat capacity, stream enthalpy, $K$-values

Interactive — click a stream number

Reading a stream table

Illustrative values consistent with the BFD balance (75% conversion per pass, ~97% overall).

Process flow diagram

Why the PFD exists

Plant design basis

Shows feedstock, product and main stream flowrates and operating conditions.

Scope of process

Defines where the process starts and stops — what is inside the battery limit.

Equipment configuration

Shows graphically the arrangement of major equipment, process lines and main control loops.

These three purposes explain every inclusion and every omission on the next slides.

Process flow diagram

What is deliberately left off the PFD

  • Minor process lines not used in normal operation, and minor equipment such as block valves and safety/relief valves.
  • Elevation of equipment.
  • All spare equipment.
  • Heat exchangers, pumps, compressors in parallel or series — shown as one unit.
  • Instrumentation not related to automatic control.
  • Instrumentation of the trip system — it cannot be decided at PFD stage.
  • Drivers of rotating machinery, except where they matter for a process control line.
  • Any dimensional information on equipment, such as internals.

Interactive — decide for each item

Does it belong on the PFD?

Shell-and-tube exchanger E-101 with its duty
Yes. It changes temperature — major equipment.
Manual block valve at a pump suction
No. Minor equipment — a P&ID item.
Control valve in a main control loop
Yes. The PFD shows main control loops; all other instrumentation waits for the P&ID.
Safety relief valve set pressure
No. Relief valves and their set pressures are P&ID content.
Elevation of the reflux drum
No. Elevations are excluded — they appear on the P&ID and elevation diagrams.
Installed spare pump P-101 B
No. Spares are omitted; parallel units are drawn as one.
Cooling water to the overhead condenser
Yes. Utility streams serving a process function are shown.
Stream 4: 654 °C, 25 bar, vapour fraction 1.0
Yes. Process conditions per stream are required information.

Note for PFD development

Paper is the cheapest place to change your mind

Process work on paper is much cheaper than project work. Changes at the PFD stage are far more economical than changes at a later stage.
Spend more time finalising the PFD before moving into the basic engineering phase.

A production PFD: towers, exchangers, pumps, tags, stream flags.

Piping & Instrumentation Diagram

The P&ID is the design basis for the EPC contractor

  • Design basis for EPC contractors, with special notes for design.
  • Equipment design basis.
  • Piping design basis — lines for normal operation, start-up and shut-down.
  • Instrumentation design basis.
  • Interlock, safeguarding and safety equipment design basis.
  • Utility design basis.
Show every component you want to see in your plant — and that you do not want the EPC contractor to miss.

Piping & Instrumentation Diagram

P&ID content

Equipment

  • All equipment, including installed stand-by
  • Titles of towers and reactors
  • Dimensions of towers, vessels, tanks
  • Vessel elevations
  • Pumps, compressors and their drivers

Piping

  • All piping with line numbers, sizes, specification
  • All valves
  • All packaged equipment with tie-ins
  • Sample connections

Instrumentation

  • All instrumentation with function types
  • In-line instrument sizes
  • Control valve sizes and action on air failure
  • Relief valves with size and set pressure

Piping & Instrumentation Diagram

What "every component" actually looks like

One vessel. Every line numbered and sized, every valve drawn, every instrument tagged.

Comparison

PFD vs P&ID

Does the diagram…PFDP&ID
get used during construction?NoYes*
show all process and service piping?NoYes
indicate all controls?NoYes
show all motors?NoYes
show thermal insulation?NoYes
show major equipment?YesYes
show flow quantities?YesNo
show stream compositions?YesNo
The PFD is needed early, when the mass balance is being prepared.
The PFD guides the preparation of the P&ID — never the other way round.

* the P&ID is the construction reference; the PFD stays the process reference.

Piping & Instrumentation Diagram

What is the P&ID based on?

Nothing above a level can be decided before the level below it is fixed. The P&ID sits on top of the whole design.
BFDBlock Flow Diagram PFDProcess Flow Diagram UFDUtility Flow Diagram HMBHeat and Material Balance

Beyond the three

Additional diagrams a project needs

  • Utility flowsheet (UFD)
  • Plot plans and elevation diagrams
  • Piping isometrics
  • Vessel sketches
  • Logic ladder diagrams
  • Wiring diagrams
  • Site plans
  • Structural support diagrams

A schematic diagram compresses conditions and tray counts onto one readable picture.

Section summary

Lecture 1-4 — what to carry forward

1

BFD → PFD → P&ID is one drawing at three levels of detail, in that order.

2

Major equipment changes $T$, $P$ or composition. Everything else waits for the P&ID.

3

Tag XX-YZZ A/B = class, area, item, parallel units. Streams get a numbered diamond.

4

PFD omissions are deliberate: no spares, no block or relief valves, no elevations, parallel units as one.

Casework 1-4 · exam-style

Turn this PFD segment into a P&ID

You are handed the PFD segment on the right: feed pump P-101 → preheater E-101 → reactor R-101 → tower T-101 with condenser and reboiler.
List what you must add to issue it as a P&ID.
  • Installed stand-by P-101 B with its own suction/discharge valves
  • Block valves and check valves around every pump
  • Control valve on the tower bottoms with a LIC loop, plus air-failure action
  • PSV-101 on the reactor with size and set pressure
  • All instruments: TI, PI, FI, analysers with function types
  • Line numbers, sizes and specification on every line
  • Vessel dimensions and elevations; drivers of rotating machinery
  • Start-up and shut-down lines; sample and drain connections; insulation

And note what you remove: flow quantities and stream compositions do not belong on a P&ID.

Lecture 1

Key Takeaways

1

Define a chemical process by the structure change and the purity lift — and remember it is always multistep.

2

Separate the process (five sections) from the plant (process + storage + utilities + waste).

3

Add detail one layer at a time: box → BFD → PFD → datasheets + P&ID → drawings.

4

Quote the estimate class with every number — accuracy comes from definition, not from confidence.

5

Finalise the PFD before basic engineering. Paper is the cheapest place to change your mind.
